newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair names top ministers in new government.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair names top ministers in new government.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair, fresh from a landslide election victory, wasted no time on Friday in naming the senior ministers of a Labour government that he said would unite Britain after 18 years of Conservative rule.
Blair's defeated rival, John Major, shocked colleagues by announcing that he would resign as leader of the Conservatives after the party lost its first election since 1974.
Greeting ecstatic, flag-waving party workers outside the prime minister's Downing Street office, Blair promised "a government of practical measures in pursuit of noble causes".
"We have secured a mandate to bring this nation together, to unite as one Britain, one nation," said Blair, at 43 the youngest prime minister this century.
"For 18 years, 18 long years, my party has been in opposition. It could only say, it could not do. Today we are charged with the deep responsibility of government.
"Today, enough of talking. It is time now to do."

Blair swiftly confirmed deputy Labour leader John Prescott would be deputy prime minister and that Gordon Brown, the intellectual force behind his single-minded transformation of Labour into a centrist party, would be finance minister.
Robin Cook, a wiry, red-bearded Scot with one of the sharpest minds in parliament, was named foreign secretary.

David Blunkett, Britain's first blind minister, will head Blair's drive to make education the passion of his government, and Margaret Beckett will be the most senior woman in the cabinet in charge of trade and industry.

Blair named Jack Straw as his interior minister and Lord Derry Irvine, his former boss when he trained to be a barrister, as Lord Chancellor, Britain's senior legal officer. None of the appointments was a surprise.
Major had earlier left Downing Street for the last time to hand in his resignation to Queen Elizabeth at Buckingham Palace after bidding an emotional farewell to his office staff.
"When the curtain falls it is time to get off the stage," he told reporters. The Conservative Party had been in power since Margaret Thatcher was elected in 1979.
The timing of Major's resignation is uncertain -- he could stay until July -- but the news sparked an immediate battle for his succession.

Kenneth Clarke, Major's finance minister, was the first to throw his hat into the ring. Former deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine and former Welsh secretary William Hague were the bookmakers' favourites.
With just one seat to be counted, Labour had 419 seats and was expected to have a majority of 179, allowing Blair to govern without looking over his shoulder for the next five years.
Turnout among the 44 million voters was 71.3 percent -- a record post-war low. In the 1992 election, 77.7 percent of the electorate voted.
In a telling sign of how Labour under Blair has won over even the sceptical financial markets, leading shares scaled new peaks and the pound recovered early losses to end the day buoyantly.
The Conservative defeat was on a scale unseen for 165 years with seven cabinet ministers, including Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, losing their seats.
Major, who was re-elected in his safe Huntingdon constituency, looked shocked by the scale of the defeat as he arrived at Conservative headquarters in London.
"Tonight we have been comprehensively defeated. Let us not pretend to ourselves it was anything other than what it was."
As Blair paid tribute to his predecessor's dignity and "essential decency", Major went to watch a cricket match, taking the same advice he had given to his disappointed supporters.
"So right, okay, we lost. Go away for the weekend, relax and then fire yourself up because when you come back we have got a job!" he told them.
Former prime minister Thatcher congratulated Blair but warned him she would watch to ensure he did not fritter away the legacy of 18 years of Conservative rule.
The Conservatives were projected to win 31 percent of the vote, down from 42.8 percent at the 1992 election, with Labour jumping to 45 percent from 35.2 percent.
Major's appeal to voters, after 18 years of Conservative rule, was "better the devil you know than the devil you don't", but voters were simply hungry for change.
They punished the Conservatives for years of internal party civil war over ties with Europe, broken tax promises, a deep recession and a wave of scandals inside the party.
The Liberal Democrats, Britain's third party, achieved their greatest breakthrough in 60 years. After winning just 20 seats in 1992, they will end up with 45 or 46 seats in the new parliament.
